en: In the *Tārāsādhana* titled *The Instruction for Deceiving Death*:
Having arisen during the morning twilight in a delightful place on the earth, sitting upon a soft seat, one should [visualize] within one's own heart a moon mandala. (Mvupts 1)
The first [syllable] of the fifth [group], joined with the second vowel,
conjoined with the half-moon and the bindu, and adorned with white rays.
Having drawn Tārā into the sky with his white rays,
she appeared with two arms, her body white, holding a boon-granting gesture and a blue lotus.
Having worshipped with devotion by means of the fivefold offerings,
one should thereafter perform the confession of sins and the rejoicing in merit.
One should likewise perform the dedication of merit and the going for refuge to the Three Jewels, and recite: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness. (Mvupts 5)
Thus, the yogi who knows the ritual procedure, having meditated upon himself as empty of self and other,
[should visualize himself] upon a moon-disk seat situated in the center of a white lotus.
One should visualize the delightful Goddess Tārā, arisen from the seed-syllable previously mentioned,
seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, and holding the gesture of granting boons and a blue lotus.
Having the form of the autumn moonbeams, seated upon a moon at her back,
complete with all ornaments, and possessing the body of a sixteen-year-old.

Having meditated upon Noble Tārā, the mother of all the Perfect Buddhas and their sons, who possesses a body capable of assuming any form at will, one should visualize her wheel of white radiance within the heart.
The eight-square grid is filled with eight syllables;
the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is placed at the center, with *oṃ* and *hāḥ* situated between the consonants at the navel.
With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, he should meditate for six months;
with an undaunted mind, he should recite this ten-syllable mantra. (Mvupts 11)
Having placed the syllable Oṃ at the beginning, one should subsequently employ Tāre;
then there should be Tuttāre, followed by Ture, ending with Svāhā—this is the mantra for all rites.
Even by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Moon, the Sun, Rudra, the guardians of the quarters, and Kāmadeva,
he whose hair-tips remain unshaken conquers death like one who is liberated.
It brings about the complete destruction of wrinkles, graying hair, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
it is the eradicator of the mass of suffering caused by the eight great fears, such as lions and the like.
The acquisition of food, drink, mansions, clothing, and so forth without having asked for them;
and the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, and the auspicious jar.
Poetic skill, eloquence, intelligence, and utterly pure wisdom, as well as other desired accomplishments, arise from this wheel. (Mvupts 16)
The *Tārāsādhana*: Instructions for Deceiving Death is completed.
